newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia assistant treasurer quits over bank stake.
newsitem.headline: Australia assistant treasurer quits over bank stake.

text.p: Australian assistant treasurer Jim Short, the junior minister responsible for banking policy, resigned on Sunday following controversy over his ownership of shares in a major bank, Prime Minister John Howard announced.
"The assistant treasurer, Senator Jim Short, has tendered his resignation from the ministry," Howard said in a statement.
"I have accepted that resignation," he added.
Howard said later that there was no connection between Short's position and that of Treasurer Peter Costello, who acknowleged on Saturday that his wife also owned bank shares.

After the holding was highlighted in The Sydney Morning Herald newspaper, Costello issued a statement on Saturday defending his wife's right to hold the shares as "an independent, professional person who is entitled to, and does, make her own decisions".
Howard last week said he had considered sacking Short for failing to reveal that his family company held shares in Australia and New Zealand Banking Group Ltd (ANZ).
Howard then said he decided not to sack Short for breaching ministerial guidelines because he considered the shareholding to be an oversight.

Under the ministerial guidelines drawn up by Howard's government, ministers are required to divest themselves of all shares and similar interests in any company or business involved in the area of their portfolio responsibilities.
However, more information came to light on the weekend when Short told Howard his office had discovered that in June he had given routine approval for a bank licence for an ANZ subsidiary.
"Now that my attention has been drawn to that approval, I feel that the circumstances of the matter have changed," Short said in a resignation letter released by Howard.
Howard said on Sunday: "At all times he has behaved with honesty and integrity. Not even his harshest critics in recent days have said that he lacked either of these qualities."
Short, 59, said last week he had taken steps to dispose of his 6,679 shares, worth about A$48,000 (US$38,000) based on Friday's closing price on the stock exchange.
Howard said Short's position in the ministry would be taken by Rod Kemp, a senator from Victoria and brother of David Kemp, junior minister for schools, vocational education and training.
Howard later told reporters in Sydney he believed Costello had behaved impeccably and that his wife's shareholding was totally above-board.
"The shares his wife bought were bought in 1994 and they were put on a public register in 1994," he said.

"Completely in accordance with the guidelines, when there was another tranche of Commonwealth Bank shares after the election, Peter asked his wife not to participate in the issue," he said. "She has behaved impeccably and so has he."
Asked whether Costello had breached any guidelines, Howard said: "No. He certainly hasn't".
Costello said on Saturday he had registered his wife's interest in a package of Commonwealth Bank shares worth about A$2,000 to the appropriate parliamentary register in March 1994.
"She purchased here CBA shares in 1994 from her own earnings. She owns there shares. She is the only one that can sell them," Costello said.
"The ministerial guidelines do no require my wife to sell her shares and I cannot divest her of her property," he said.
"I have adhered strictly to the ministerial guidelines."
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 373-1800
